cards.front: What is type coercion in JS, and how do === / == / + / if (x) differ?
cards.meaning: JavaScript automatically converts a value because an operator or API asked for another kind. === compares without converting types. == converts first (abstract equality). +, -, and if (x) also coerce, each with different rules. Interview goal: predict common results and defend === by default — not recite the whole spec.

cards.front: All falsy values — and Boolean([]) / {} / '0' / 'false' / new Boolean(false)?
cards.meaning: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy: [], {}, '0', 'false', ' ' (non-empty string). Boolean(new Boolean(false)) is true — object wrappers are truthy even when they wrap false.
cards.example: Boolean([]); // true  Boolean('0'); // true  Boolean(new Boolean(false)); // true

cards.front: 0 || 'default' vs 0 ?? 'default' — and why if (value) is dangerous?
cards.meaning: || / if (x) use truthiness: 0 and '' are falsy so they take the fallback. ?? only treats null/undefined as missing — 0 stays 0, '' stays ''. APIs returning 0 or '' as real data break if (value); check explicitly (value == null, value === 0, value.length === 0).

cards.front: Number('  12 '), Number(''), Number('12px'), Number(null), Number(undefined); String(null)?
cards.meaning: 12, 0, NaN, 0, NaN. Whitespace around digits is accepted; empty string becomes 0; junk suffix is NaN; null is 0; undefined is NaN. String(null) is 'null'; String(undefined) is 'undefined' — not empty string.
parseInt('12px', 10) → 12 (parses a numeric prefix). Number('12px') → NaN. Different tools, different jobs.

Different types → false immediately (1 === '1', true === 1, null === undefined are all false). Same type → compare with no coercion. Still: NaN !== NaN; +0 === -0. So === is “no coercion,” not perfect mathematical identity.
null == undefined is true (the only loose pair). null == 0, undefined == 0, and null == false are all false — null/undefined only loosely equal each other (and themselves).
cards.example: null == undefined; // true  null == 0; // false  null == false; // false

cards.meaning: All true. Number ↔ string: the string converts to number ('' → 0, '0' → 0, '1' → 1). Boolean coerces to number (false → 0, true → 1), then numeric compare — so 1 == true is also true.
cards.example: 1 == '1'; // true  0 == ''; // true  0 == false; // true  '0' == false; // true

cards.meaning: Both true. ![] is false because the array is truthy. Then [] == false: false → 0; [] ToPrimitive → '' → 0; so 0 == 0. Truthiness and primitive coercion are different steps.
cards.notes: Walk the chain in interviews; default to === in code.

cards.front: How does + choose concat vs add — and do - / * concatenate?
cards.meaning: After ToPrimitive: if either operand is a string → concatenation; else both to numbers and add. So 1+'1' is '11'; true+true is 2. -, *, / always go numeric: '5'-1 is 4; '5'*'2' is 10. Only + concatenates.

Objects become primitives via ToPrimitive (valueOf / toString) before numeric/string coercion finishes. Usual: {} → '[object Object]'; [] → ''; [1,2] → '1,2'. So 1 + [] is '1'; [] + {} is '[object Object]'; +[] is 0; +{} is NaN. Explains [1] == 1 and [1,2] == '1,2'.

cards.front: Why does x === NaN never work — Number.isNaN vs isNaN?
cards.meaning: NaN means “invalid number”; IEEE-754 makes it unequal to everything, including itself. Use Number.isNaN(x) — no coercion. Global isNaN('foo') is true because it coerces the string to NaN first. Prefer Number.isFinite over global isFinite for the same reason.
cards.example: NaN === NaN; // false  Number.isNaN('foo'); // false  isNaN('foo'); // true

cards.meaning: Same except Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true and Object.is(+0, -0) is false; === treats +0 and -0 as equal. Day-to-day equality is still === plus Number.isNaN when checking NaN. Use Object.is when NaN identity or +0 vs -0 matters.
cards.example: Object.is(NaN, NaN); // true  Object.is(+0, -0); // false  +0 === -0; // true

cards.meaning: Deliberate shorthand for value === null || value === undefined. Otherwise prefer === in app code.
cards.example: if (x == null) return 'missing'; // null or undefined

cards.meaning: <, >, <=, >= also coerce (often ToNumber / ToPrimitive). When both sides become strings, comparison is lexicographic: '10' > '9' is false (character comparison); 10 > '9' is true (numeric). Another reason not to mix types casually.

cards.front: Where should you convert types, and are == puzzles a style to copy?
cards.meaning: Convert explicitly at system boundaries (e.g. Number(req.query.page)). Use === / !==; value == null only as a deliberate nullish check. Don't use truthiness to validate numbers that can be 0 or strings that can be ''. Treat == puzzles as interview literacy, not app style.
It reduces accidental mixed-type == at compile time, but runtime JS coercion still exists at boundaries (query params, JSON, APIs). Types do not convert values.
